A year of daily speaking practice: what actually changes

A year of daily practice can change how you speak, but nobody can promise a level by a date. Here is what actually changes, and what it takes.

Published September 10, 2023 · 11 min read · Sławomir Onyszko ·Updated November 14, 2026

Many promises about learning a language in a year start with a number and end with a level. They skip the only part that matters: what you do every day.

A year is a useful frame for practice. It is not a guarantee. The result depends on where you start, which language you are learning, how often you practice, and whether the practice makes you speak or only recognize.

I know this from both sides. I could read and understand a lot before I could speak. The first time I tried to say something in a real conversation, my head went quiet. The words were there, but they did not come out. What changed was not a hidden method. It was daily practice: I spoke, I got corrections, and I returned to them in review.

My English teacher had studied the language her whole life. She knew grammar better than I did. And yet, in class, we rarely spoke our own sentences. School spends years on language but rarely teaches speaking.

A year is a frame, not a guarantee

A year gives you many short sessions. It gives you enough repetitions to build a habit, enough mistakes to see a pattern, and enough corrections to notice what you actually need to work on.

A year does not give you a level by itself. Three people can practice for a year and end up in very different places. One may speak in short sentences about familiar topics. Another may handle a work meeting. A third may still freeze. The difference is not talent. It is what they did in those sessions.

What happens in those 15 minutes

Imagine two people with the same 15 minutes a day.

The first person opens an app, picks the right answer from four options, keeps a streak, and feels productive. The second person says a sentence out loud, gets a correction, writes down what went wrong, and reviews the correction a few days later.

After a year, the first person has practiced recognition. The second person has practiced speaking. Recognition helps you understand. Speaking helps you speak. They are different skills.

You can recognize a song after two chords. Singing it is a different job. Language works the same way. Knowing the word is not the same as building a sentence with it under pressure.

Five things that make practice work

You can practice every day and see no difference if the practice does not touch the right mechanisms. These five matter.

Deliberate practice. Do not practice what you already know. Work on what you cannot say. If you always talk about the weather, try to talk about your job or a conflict. Deliberate practice is uncomfortable, but it moves the boundary.

Active recall. Instead of reading a word again, try to remember it from memory. The difficulty is part of the method. Your brain practices retrieving, not recognizing.

Connecting to what you know. A new word is easier to remember when you connect it to an image, a sound, your own experience, or a sentence about yourself. A word that is about you has more paths back.

Spaced review. Return to a word or correction when you are about to forget it. Easy items come back later, hard ones sooner. The system chooses the time.

Personalization. You remember what is about you more easily. That is why a sentence about your own day works better than a textbook sentence about someone else.

Speaking combines all five

When you say your own sentence, you do several things at once. You recall words, connect them to what you know, notice what is missing, and talk about yourself. That is why speaking is so effective: it does not train one mechanism, it trains several at once.

You can learn words in isolation, but only a sentence shows whether you can use them. You can review flashcards, but only speaking shows whether the word comes out under pressure.

What you do every day

Daily practice does not have to be complicated. It has four steps: a few words, one sentence out loud, one correction, and one review.

Words are the building blocks. Pick a few common words or words you need. Flashcards with active recall and spaced review help you keep them.

Then you say your own sentence out loud. That is the moment when a word becomes a skill. A correction tells you what you said, what a more natural version is, and why. Review brings it back before it disappears.

It is not a complicated system. It is a small loop you can repeat.

What a daily session looks like

A typical session is 10 to 15 minutes. You open the app and see what is there: a few words, a speaking exercise, a correction, and review.

You read a short story at your level and on topics you chose. The story is optional, but it gives you context and input. You answer a speaking exercise and get a transcript, a corrected version, and an explanation. You learn a few words by writing your own sentences with them. You review the cards the system picked for today.

There is no appointment, no audience, and no need to summon courage for a video call. You can do it alone, at home, on an ordinary evening.

The daily goal can be set to 5, 10, 15, 30, or 60 minutes. The session is short on purpose. A short session you repeat is more useful than one long session you do once and abandon.

What changes early, and what changes later

The first changes are usually small. You freeze less often. You can say a sentence without stopping in the middle. You start noticing your own mistakes. You remember a correction from last week.

Later, sentences get longer. Conversation becomes easier. You can explain an idea, tell a story, or handle a problem. Your pronunciation becomes easier to understand.

No one can promise a level by a date. A B2 certificate in a year, a fluent conversation in three months, a native accent: those are not plans. They are hopes with a date attached.

Accent is part of who you are. The goal is not to sound like someone else. The goal is to be understood without extra effort from the listener.

What a year cannot do

A year of daily practice cannot replace real conversation. A tutor or a patient friend is still the best way to practice spontaneity, interruptions, jokes, and the messy parts of a real conversation. A good tutor remains the standard.

A year of daily practice can give you the foundation that makes those conversations easier. It can make you less afraid to start. It can give you the sentences and corrections you need to keep going.

It will not remove your accent, and it should not try. It will not guarantee a certificate, and it should not pretend to. It will not do the work for you. It can make the work easier to repeat.

Fit it into a real day

You do not need a perfect schedule. You need a few decisions that reduce friction.

  • Limit social media during the time you set aside for practice.
  • Turn on focus mode for 15 minutes.
  • Plan the session at a specific point in the day, for example after coffee.
  • If you do not have 15 minutes, split the session into two shorter ones.
  • Use time you already lose: the commute, a queue, a break.
  • Learn while moving if you do not like sitting at a desk.

These are six simple strategies. You do not have to use all of them. Pick two that fit your day.

Four rules for speaking

  • Start simple. One sentence about yourself is better than a perfect sentence you never say.
  • Speak as much as you can. Short sentences, repetition, and mistakes are part of practice.
  • Practice regularly. 5 minutes every day works better than an hour once a week.
  • Do not fear mistakes. A mistake you hear and understand is material for a correction.

Keep learning beyond the app

The app is not the whole language. Talk to people, listen, read, and learn grammar when you need it.

A conversation with a person gives you chaos, pauses, and spontaneity that an app cannot offer. Listening and reading give you input and models. Grammar helps you understand why something sounds the way it does.

You do not have to do everything at once. Pick one thing outside the app and do it regularly.

What Soliloquy is

Soliloquy means speaking your thoughts aloud when you are alone. That is where the app's name comes from.

Inside, you have a lexicon of the most common words, flashcards with active recall and spaced review, and speaking with correction. Words from the lexicon and stories go into one deck. When you speak, you get a transcript, a corrected version, and an explanation. You can save a correction as a card. The system chooses when to bring a word back.

Stories are optional input. They give you context and vocabulary, but they are not a requirement. You can start with a few words and one sentence.

How to judge progress without a streak

A streak is a nudge. It is not a grade. It tells you that you showed up. It does not tell you that you spoke.

Better signs of progress:

  • You can say more sentences about your day than you could a month ago.
  • You understand a correction the first time you see it.
  • You remember a word from a story without looking it up.
  • You can handle a speaking exercise that used to feel hard.
  • You can hear the difference between what you said and what you meant to say.

These are small, concrete signs. They are more useful than a number that only counts taps.

If you miss a few days

You will miss days. A plan that only works when everything goes perfectly is not a plan.

When you come back, the app shows what is due and what to review first. Your progress is saved. You do not start from zero. You return to daily practice. The goal is not a perfect streak. The goal is a practice you can return to.

How to start without a big plan

You do not need a one-year plan, a stack of books, or a perfect schedule. You need one small loop you can repeat.

  1. Pick a language you actually want to use.
  2. Set a daily goal you can keep, even on a busy day.
  3. Read something at your level or pick a few words.
  4. Say something out loud and get a correction.
  5. Return to what you learned before it disappears.

Soliloquy sets this up in 2 to 3 minutes. You choose your language, level, motivation, and topics. Then today's practice is ready.

Hard questions

Can I reach B2 in a year?

No one can promise that. It depends on your starting point, the language, how much you practice, and what you do in that practice. Daily practice gives you a real chance to improve. A date on a calendar does not guarantee it.

Do I need a tutor?

A tutor is the best way to practice real conversation. Soliloquy is not a replacement for a tutor. It is a way to speak, get corrections, and review them every day, so you can bring more to conversations with a person.

What if I miss a week?

You return. Your progress and corrections are still there. The app shows what to review first. Missing a week is not a failure. It is a week.

Can AI replace a person?

In some things, it cannot. Real conversation gives you chaos, pauses, and spontaneity that AI cannot offer. AI is good at something else: it is available when you want to practice, it does not get tired of your mistakes, and it does not need an appointment. It is not either-or.

A year is enough to build the habit

A year will not guarantee a level. It is enough to build a daily practice, collect a record of your mistakes, and see what changes when you speak instead of only recognizing.

If you want to check whether this loop works for you, open the trial. Do one session: pick a few words, say one sentence out loud, and ask for one correction. Look at the correction. If it shows you something useful, you have your answer.
